To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

neurons in parieto-frontal cortex, the superior colliculus, and the basal ganglia encode the expected value of a target, and that posterior cingulate neurons encode the value of a target after it has been visited.

(a) the value of an action is represented by neurons in a distributed network of brain areas; (b) these areas include the superior colliculus, parietal cortex and prefrontal cortex; (c) the value of the action is updated based on reward outcomes, as signaled by neurons in the midbrain; (d) the value of actions is used to guide the selection of appropriate behavior, as signaled by posterior cingulate neurons.

neurons in a distributed neural network encode the expected value of a reward associated with the location of visual stimuli, and that the brain uses this information to guide the generation of appropriate oculomotor behaviors in order to obtain the reward.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the representation of value in the primate nervous system.
the representation of behavioral value, and the neural processes by which this representation is updated as reward contingences change.
how the brain computes the value of actions, and how this computation is linked to the selection of actions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain has evolved to be a value-based decision-making device.
reward-related signals are represented in many brain areas, but that the specific roles of these areas are still unclear.
a distributed network of brain areas is responsible for the processing of reward information in order to update the behavioral value of stimuli in the environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the primate brain represents the behavioral value of objects, and that this value is updated in real time in response to changes in reward contingencies.
the brain represents the value of actions and the outcomes of those actions.
we are trying to understand how the brain makes decisions about what to do next.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, at least in primates, reward information is encoded by multiple brain structures in a manner that is both spatially and temporally precise.
the brain is not only able to learn the value of stimuli in the environment, but also able to update that value in real time.
the brain represents behavioral value as a function of the reward history and the expected outcome of a given action.
